summary.title: Programming Languages That Blew My Mind
summary.one_liner: A personal, chronological tour of programming languages (BASIC, Turbo Pascal, assembly, HyperCard, OCaml, Java, Prolog, Coq, Erlang, pi-calculus, Opalang, Rust) and the specific ideas each one introduced to the author.
keywords: languages that changed how i think about programming
takeaways: Many modern language features (generics, pattern matching, garbage collection, type inference) were present in older languages like OCaml and Prolog.
Prolog and Coq change thinking: you describe rules or specifications rather than algorithms, and types can act as proofs.
Erlang's actor model, distribution and 'let it fail' design influenced later systems such as Scala, Go and microservices.
Rust's type system can encode safety properties (e.g. affine types for typestate), shifting effort toward thinking before coding.
Opalang explored single-codebase multi-tier programming, automatically splitting client, server and database code.
summary.summary: The author, a long-time programmer, walks through languages that most changed their view of programming, in the order they were discovered: BASIC, Turbo Pascal, assembly, HyperCard, OCaml, Java, Prolog, Coq, Erlang, the pi-calculus, Opalang and Rust. Each section lists "mind blown" moments, such as OCaml's type inference and pattern matching, Prolog's rule-based programming, or Rust's affine types and friendly tooling. The post also traces how these ideas later appeared in other languages and reflects on the limits of languages that were ahead of their time. It is an opinion essay with anecdotes rather than a tutorial, and it ends by asking readers which languages influenced them.
